messages.content: I want to design an incremental cross-module optimizer that preserves the benefits of optimization while keeping cache reuse sound under symbol interposition. The design needs to match clean-build semantics under dependency changes, dynamic symbol interposition, and mixtures of optimized and unoptimized modules. For single-module edits, the target is to halve full-LTO rebuild time while keeping runtime within 5% of full LTO.

That sets both a correctness requirement and a performance target. Reused optimization results must remain semantically valid across the three stated conditions. At the same time, single-module edits should take at most half the full-LTO rebuild time, with the resulting runtime no more than 5% above full LTO's runtime under a comparable measurement.
What does “sound cache reuse” mean here? Is it just a matter of checking whether the edited module changed?

No. A cached cross-module result may depend on information beyond the module where the result is stored. Sound reuse means that the assumptions relevant to that result still hold when it is reused. Whether one module's contents are unchanged is not, by itself, enough to establish that a result involving other modules remains valid.
So dependency changes are relevant even when the source I am editing is somewhere else?

Yes. The requirement to match clean-build semantics under dependency changes applies to the resulting build, not just to the edited module in isolation. A dependency change may matter to an optimization that used information from that dependency. The design has to distinguish reuse that remains valid from reuse whose supporting assumptions need to be reconsidered; the goal does not prescribe a particular mechanism for doing so.
How should I read “match clean-build semantics”? Does that require identical build artifacts?

The stated requirement is semantic: the incremental result should behave as a clean build would for the relevant inputs and conditions. It does not, on its own, specify byte-for-byte identical artifacts or identical internal optimization decisions. The point is that caching must not change the program's meaning relative to a clean build.
Why call out dynamic symbol interposition separately from ordinary dependency changes?

It makes symbol binding an explicit part of the correctness challenge. A cross-module optimization can be unsound if it treats a symbol's target as fixed when interposition can change which definition is used. Sound cache reuse therefore cannot rely on a binding assumption unless that assumption remains justified in the conditions where the cached result is used.
Could the optimizer simply assume interposition will not happen to reach the rebuild-time target?

Not while satisfying this goal. Matching clean-build semantics under dynamic symbol interposition is an explicit requirement. The rebuild-time target cannot be met by setting that correctness condition aside.
And what does the mixed optimized/unoptimized-modules condition add?

It means correctness must not depend on every participating module receiving the same optimization treatment. Cross-module work and cache reuse have to remain semantically sound when optimized and unoptimized modules are present together. The requirement does not say that every module must be optimized, or that optimization choices must be identical across modules.
Is the aim to avoid all cross-module optimizations whenever there is uncertainty?

That would miss the stated aim of preserving optimization benefits. The desired balance is to retain cross-module optimization where its assumptions are valid, while not reusing a result when its assumptions no longer support it. This describes the design objective rather than choosing a particular optimization or cache policy.
Could you separate the two numerical targets? I do not want to conflate build time with program runtime.

For single-module edits, the rebuild-time target is half the time of a full-LTO rebuild. Separately, the runtime target is within 5% of full LTO. The first concerns the time to rebuild after an edit; the second concerns the runtime of what was built. Neither figure, by itself, establishes semantic correctness.
If an edit changes a dependency rather than a single module, does the half-time target still apply?

The wording assigns that quantitative rebuild-time target to single-module edits. Dependency changes are explicitly covered by the clean-build-semantics requirement, but no separate rebuild-time percentage is stated for them. It would be an extrapolation to claim the half-time target for every dependency-change case.
Would it be accurate to say that a cache hit is beneficial only if it also remains semantically valid?

Yes. A fast cache hit that produces behavior different from a clean build would not satisfy the goal. Conversely, rejecting every reusable result could protect correctness but work against the incremental rebuild-time and optimization aims. The design has to address both sides without treating one as a substitute for the other.
I am trying to phrase the key risk without prescribing an implementation. Is it that previously valid cross-module information can stop being valid?

That is a fair high-level description. A cached result may reflect facts about dependencies or symbol binding that need not hold after conditions change. The soundness question is whether the result's relevant assumptions still apply at reuse time. That framing leaves open how an optimizer records, checks, or responds to those assumptions.
Does “within 5% of full LTO” mean the incremental result has to match full LTO's runtime exactly?

No. It allows a runtime difference of up to 5% against the full-LTO runtime baseline. Since runtime is elapsed execution time, a result taking no more than 1.05 times the full-LTO runtime would be within that upper bound. The requirement does not demand identical generated code or exactly equal runtime.
There are two references to full LTO, then: one for rebuilding and one for runtime?

Right. Full-LTO rebuild time is the comparison for the single-module-edit speed target. Full-LTO runtime is the comparison for the resulting program's runtime target. Clean-build semantics supplies the correctness comparison under dependency changes, dynamic symbol interposition, and mixed optimized/unoptimized modules.
Can the design promise the time and runtime targets just by describing how cache reuse should work?

A description can state how the design intends to preserve valid optimization work and avoid unsound reuse, but it cannot establish that the numerical targets have been achieved. Halving full-LTO rebuild time for single-module edits and staying within 5% of full-LTO runtime are targets to assess, not results already demonstrated by the goal statement.
What should a concise statement of the design objective emphasize, then?

Design an incremental cross-module optimizer that reuses optimization work only when doing so preserves clean-build semantics, including under dependency changes, dynamic symbol interposition, and mixed optimized/unoptimized modules. Preserve enough optimization benefit that, for single-module edits, rebuilding takes half the full-LTO rebuild time while the resulting runtime stays within 5% of full LTO.

As a concrete proposal, cache imported IR using dependency digests, symbol-resolution maps, and optimization modes, then selectively reoptimize dependents while preserving preemptible calls. How do those pieces fit together?

The cached imported IR is reusable only when the information it relied on remains applicable. Dependency digests represent dependency state, symbol-resolution maps represent relevant symbol-resolution information, and optimization modes distinguish the conditions under which the IR was optimized. If a relevant condition changes, the proposal is to reoptimize affected dependents selectively rather than automatically redo all cross-module work. Preserving preemptible calls keeps that reuse and reoptimization from treating a potentially interposed call as though its destination were unconditionally fixed.
Why cache imported IR rather than describe the cache as holding a whole finished build?

Imported IR is the specific cross-module material named in the proposal. Describing the cache at that level makes the reuse decision about imported information and its assumptions, while leaving room for selective reoptimization of dependents. The proposal does not specify that an entire finished build can be reused as one indivisible object.
What role do dependency digests play? Would an unchanged importer be enough to justify a hit?

Not necessarily. An unchanged importer may have used information from a dependency whose state has changed. Dependency digests give the reuse decision a way to account for dependency state rather than looking only at the importer. The proposal does not specify exactly how those digests are computed or which changes they distinguish, so their use still has to be sound for the dependencies that matter to the cached IR.
And the symbol-resolution maps are a different kind of condition?

Yes. A dependency digest and a symbol-resolution map describe different aspects of the conditions surrounding imported IR. The map matters because a cross-module optimization can depend on which symbol a reference resolves to. Checking it helps avoid reusing an assumption about symbol resolution when that assumption no longer applies. It should not be read as permission to ignore possible dynamic interposition.
I want to be careful with that last point. If the map records one resolution, can the optimizer turn every call into a direct call to that definition?

No. The proposal explicitly says to preserve preemptible calls. A recorded resolution does not, by itself, make a potentially interposed call non-preemptible. Any reuse or reoptimization must respect the call's preemptibility rather than converting a resolution observation into an unconditional binding guarantee.
What does preserving a preemptible call mean at the level of this proposal, without choosing a code-generation technique?

It means the optimization must not remove the call's relevant possibility of being resolved through interposition where that possibility is part of the required semantics. The proposal states the constraint, not a particular instruction sequence, representation, or implementation rule for every call.
Why include optimization modes in the cache conditions?

A cached imported IR result can reflect the mode in which optimization was performed. Accounting for optimization modes prevents a reuse decision from silently treating differently optimized conditions as interchangeable. That is especially pertinent to the requirement that optimized and unoptimized modules coexist without changing clean-build semantics.
Does including a mode mean an unoptimized module must be optimized before it can participate?

No. Recording optimization modes is about evaluating reuse under the applicable conditions; it does not impose uniform optimization across modules. The proposal remains compatible with a mixture of optimized and unoptimized modules, provided the resulting behavior matches clean-build semantics.
What does “selectively reoptimize dependents” commit us to?

It commits the proposal to identifying dependents whose prior cross-module optimization may be affected and reoptimizing those, instead of treating every change as a reason to reoptimize everything. It does not specify an exact dependency graph, a fixed number of affected modules, or a guarantee that only one module needs work after a single-module edit.
Could a change to one dependency require reoptimizing more than its immediate importer?

The word “dependents” does not restrict the affected work to immediate importers. If an optimization result depends, even indirectly, on information that has changed, sound reuse has to account for that dependence. How the design discovers and scopes those effects is not specified by the proposal.
Would a changed digest always force reoptimization, even if the change is irrelevant to an imported result?

The proposal does not define that granularity. A digest change can signal that cached assumptions need reconsideration, but whether a particular result can still be reused depends on what the cache conditions establish. The essential constraint is that selective reuse must be sound; the proposal does not promise that every irrelevant change is filtered out.
Is the converse also important: a digest match alone should not settle the reuse decision?

Yes. The proposal names dependency digests, symbol-resolution maps, and optimization modes together. A dependency digest match alone does not address a relevant change in symbol resolution or optimization mode. Nor does matching recorded conditions excuse violating the separate requirement to preserve preemptible calls.
Suppose I call these three items a cache key. Does that capture the proposal?

It captures the idea that they condition cache reuse, as long as “cache key” does not imply that merely comparing three labels proves every semantic assumption. The proposal says to cache imported IR by dependency digests, symbol-resolution maps, and optimization modes; soundness still requires interpreting those conditions correctly, particularly in the presence of dynamic symbol interposition.
How does the proposal try to retain cross-module optimization benefits instead of just disabling risky optimization?

It retains the possibility of reusing imported IR when its relevant conditions still hold and reoptimizing only affected dependents when they do not. That avoids making every change an automatic rejection of all previously useful cross-module work. At the same time, preserving preemptible calls sets a semantic boundary on what optimization can assume about symbol binding.
Does selective reoptimization already establish the target of halving full-LTO rebuild time for single-module edits?

No. Selective reoptimization is a proposed way to reduce rebuild work, not a measured result. The target remains to halve full-LTO rebuild time for single-module edits while keeping runtime within 5% of full LTO. This proposal does not itself demonstrate either numerical outcome.
And a faster rebuild would not justify a changed answer when a symbol is interposed?

Correct. The incremental result still needs to match clean-build semantics under dynamic symbol interposition, dependency changes, and mixtures of optimized and unoptimized modules. Preserving preemptible calls is an explicit part of this proposal for respecting that constraint; rebuild-time savings cannot replace semantic correctness.
Can I frame the proposal as reusing work when its context is still compatible, and redoing only the work whose context is affected?

Yes, with the context stated precisely: dependency digests, symbol-resolution maps, and optimization modes condition reuse of cached imported IR; affected dependents are selectively reoptimized; and preemptible calls remain preemptible. That framing expresses the proposal without claiming a particular invalidation algorithm or that its performance targets have already been met.
The unresolved part for me is visibility and binding. Which changes to a symbol's visibility or binding should invalidate cached imported IR, and which would leave a preemptible call safe to reuse?

I would frame that as an assumption question rather than classify every visibility change by name. For each cached import, we need to know whether its validity depends on a symbol being preemptible, non-preemptible, or bound to a particular definition. A change that defeats such an assumption would require reconsidering the cached result. A call that remains preemptible in the reused result might be safe with respect to a change in its eventual target, but only if no other part of that result relies on the old binding.
So the same symbol-resolution change might affect different cached results differently?

Potentially. One result might merely retain a call whose destination can be selected through interposition; another might have used information about a particular definition to optimize surrounding code. The question is whether the change alters an assumption made by each result, not simply whether the symbol's name appears in it.
Would changing a symbol from preemptible to non-preemptible necessarily make a cached preemptible call invalid?

Not necessarily on that fact alone. The important comparison is whether reusing that call and its surrounding imported IR preserves the semantics required of the clean build under the changed conditions. A previously preemptible call does not by itself assert a fixed target, but the cached result could contain other assumptions that matter. We cannot settle reuse solely from the call's presence.
What about the reverse direction, where a symbol becomes preemptible?

That direction deserves particular scrutiny if the cached result treated the symbol as bound to one definition. Once interposition must be respected, reusing an optimization that depends on fixed binding could be unsound. If the cached result already preserves a preemptible call and makes no incompatible assumption elsewhere, the binding change might not invalidate it for that reason. That is a conditional distinction, not a blanket rule for all imported IR.
Is it enough to inspect the call itself, then?

No. A call can remain visibly preemptible while an optimization elsewhere in the imported result still relies on facts about the previously expected target. The question should cover the assumptions embodied in the cached imported IR and any optimization using it, not just the apparent form of one call.
Could we phrase the boundary as ‘invalidate when the identity of the chosen definition changes’?

That may be too broad in some cases and too narrow in others. A changed chosen definition need not defeat a result that genuinely preserves dynamic selection and assumes nothing about either definition. Conversely, a change in whether fixed binding is permitted could matter to a result even before considering which definition is selected. It is more precise to ask whether the visibility or binding change invalidates an assumption on which reuse depends.
How do visibility changes fit that phrasing? Visibility is not itself the call target.

Right. Visibility can affect what binding assumptions are permissible, rather than merely naming a target. The question is whether the changed visibility alters the call's preemptibility or another property the cached import relied on. If it does, the affected result needs reassessment; if it does not, that visibility change alone may not rule out reuse.
Then ‘safe to reuse’ is narrower than ‘the cache still contains valid IR’?

It can be helpful to distinguish those ideas conceptually. Imported IR might still be meaningful as material to reconsider, while a previously optimized use of it might no longer be valid. The question here is which cached results can be reused without violating clean-build semantics. It does not yet specify whether the design stores or invalidates those pieces separately.
Suppose a call remains preemptible, but a dependency changes. Can I mark it safe based solely on preemptibility?

No. Preserving the call addresses the risk of assuming an unchangeable symbol target, but a dependency change could affect other information used by the imported IR. ‘Safe to reuse’ must still account for the result's relevant dependency, resolution, and optimization-mode conditions. Preemptibility is one necessary consideration where interposition matters, not a universal cache-validity test.
Does a changed symbol-resolution map automatically require throwing out every cached import that mentions the symbol?

The question does not establish such a blanket rule. A map change should prompt examination of results whose assumptions may depend on it. If a cached result remains valid regardless of the resolution change—for example, because it preserves the necessary preemptibility and relies on no particular definition—reuse might be possible. Whether a given result actually meets those conditions remains to be determined.
What if the map stays the same but visibility changes?

An unchanged recorded resolution would not necessarily settle it. A visibility change could alter whether an optimization is allowed to treat that resolution as fixed. The validity check needs to account for the binding assumptions relevant to the cached result, rather than treating a matching map entry as a complete proof of safety.
I want the question to cover changes in permission to assume fixed binding as well as changes in the selected target. Is that fair?

Yes. Both can matter: which definition may be reached, and whether the optimizer may assume that choice cannot be displaced. Asking about both makes the visibility-and-binding question more precise without presuming that either kind of change always invalidates every cached import.
Would you answer by listing symbols that are always safe and symbols that are always unsafe?

Not from the information here. The same symbol can appear in cached results with different assumptions, and a preemptible call can coexist with other optimized uses of imported information. A useful answer would classify the change together with what the particular cached result assumed, then determine whether reuse preserves the required semantics.
So the open question is really about the invalidation boundary, not just the vocabulary of visibility states?

Exactly. It asks where visibility or symbol-binding changes cross from a condition a cached result can tolerate into a change that invalidates its assumptions. It also asks when preserving a preemptible call is sufficient for reuse with respect to interposition—and when other assumptions in the imported IR prevent that conclusion.

Here is a hypothesis for that invalidation boundary: use per-symbol fingerprints covering visibility, version, and prevailing definition. If a fingerprint changes, invalidate dependent imports; unchanged dynamically bound calls should match clean builds. Does that answer the visibility-and-binding question?

It offers a specific answer to investigate. The fingerprint identifies three symbol properties that may matter to a cached import: visibility, version, and prevailing definition. A change to one of those properties would invalidate imports dependent on that symbol, rather than every cached import. The second part of the hypothesis is that a dynamically bound call left unchanged can still behave as it would in a clean build. Neither part is established merely by stating the hypothesis.
Why make the fingerprints per-symbol rather than describe one condition for the whole cache?

Per-symbol fingerprints express a narrower invalidation boundary. They let the hypothesis distinguish imports dependent on a changed symbol from imports that are not. That is the proposed scope of invalidation, not a claim that every dependency of every cached result has already been identified correctly.
What does “covering visibility, version, and prevailing definition” require me to keep distinct?

It means the fingerprint must account for each of those named properties, rather than standing for symbol identity alone. Visibility concerns the binding conditions associated with the symbol; version and prevailing definition are additional parts of the symbol state named by the hypothesis. A reuse decision based on this fingerprint cannot ignore a change in one of those covered properties simply because the others stayed the same.
If visibility changes but the prevailing definition does not, would the hypothesis still invalidate dependent imports?

Yes, if the visibility change changes that symbol's fingerprint. The hypothesis does not say to wait for the prevailing definition to change before invalidating dependent imports. It treats visibility as a covered property in its own right.
And if the version changes while visibility and prevailing definition remain the same?

The same reading applies: a version change reflected in the per-symbol fingerprint would invalidate dependent imports. The hypothesis names version separately, so an unchanged prevailing definition would not, by itself, make that fingerprint unchanged.
What about a new prevailing definition with the other two properties unchanged?

That too is a change to a covered property. Under the hypothesis, imports dependent on that symbol would be invalidated. The stated rule does not require visibility or version to change along with the prevailing definition.
Does “dependent imports” mean every imported IR result that merely mentions the symbol?

The hypothesis does not define dependence at that level of detail. It specifies invalidating imports dependent on the symbol when its fingerprint changes. Whether a mere mention constitutes a dependency for a particular cached result is part of what a sound interpretation of that rule would have to resolve; we should not silently equate the two.
Then is the intended distinction that a changed fingerprint does not automatically invalidate unrelated imports?

Yes. The scope stated here is dependent imports. An import unrelated to the changed symbol is not brought into that invalidation rule solely because some other symbol's fingerprint changed. That is a proposed selective boundary, not a guarantee that any particular import is unrelated.
How does this hypothesis treat a call that remains dynamically bound?

Its second claim is that an unchanged dynamically bound call matches clean-build behavior. The important qualifications are both “unchanged” and “dynamically bound”: the hypothesis is not asserting that a call transformed to rely on one fixed target would be safe, nor that every surrounding optimization is safe merely because a call remains present.
Could the prevailing definition change while the call itself stays dynamically bound and unchanged?

Those are conceptually different conditions. The prevailing definition is a property the proposed fingerprint covers; the unchanged dynamically bound call is about preserving the call's binding behavior. Under the hypothesis, a changed fingerprint would invalidate dependent imports, even though the call-level claim might still hold for a call left dynamically bound. The call-level claim does not override the stated invalidation rule.
So I should not say that every import containing a preemptible call is safe to reuse?

Correct. The hypothesis is narrower. It proposes fingerprint-based invalidation for dependent imports, alongside the expectation that unchanged dynamically bound calls match clean builds. An imported result could depend on a symbol property in addition to containing such a call; the unchanged call alone would not establish that the whole result can be reused.
Is the converse also too strong—that any change to a fingerprint must change the program's behavior?

Yes. The hypothesis says a changed fingerprint invalidates dependent imports; it does not say the program's observable behavior must change. Invalidation is a proposed precaution about reuse of cached imported IR, not a prediction that every covered symbol change produces a different runtime outcome.
If a fingerprint stays the same, does this hypothesis prove that an import is reusable?

Not by itself. An unchanged fingerprint says that the three covered symbol properties have not changed according to that fingerprint. Reuse still depends on the other relevant conditions for the imported IR. The hypothesis addresses visibility, version, prevailing definition, and unchanged dynamically bound calls; it is not a complete proof of cache validity under every dependency or optimization-mode change.
I also do not want to imply that the symbol fingerprint replaces the dependency digests and optimization modes in the proposal.

That would go beyond the hypothesis. Per-symbol fingerprints can express a proposed invalidation rule for symbol-related dependencies without displacing the other stated conditions on cached imported IR. A result could have stable symbol fingerprints yet still require reconsideration for a different relevant change.
How strongly can I phrase the clean-build part? ‘Unchanged dynamically bound calls match clean builds’ sounds definitive.

Keep its status explicit: this is the hypothesis being advanced, not an observed result. You can say, “The hypothesis is that unchanged dynamically bound calls match clean-build semantics.” That preserves the proposed claim while avoiding an assertion that it has already been verified.
Is the proposed reason for that claim simply that the call has not been pinned to the prevailing definition?

That captures the conceptual distinction without establishing the outcome. A call that remains dynamically bound has not, at the call itself, been made into an unconditional call to the prevailing definition. The hypothesis is that leaving it unchanged preserves the relevant clean-build behavior. It still leaves open whether any other cached optimization carries an incompatible assumption.
Would this hypothesis settle which visibility changes leave a preemptible call safe?

It offers a conditional boundary rather than a list of visibility states. A visibility change reflected in the fingerprint invalidates dependent imports. Separately, a call left dynamically bound and unchanged is hypothesized to match a clean build. Those statements can both apply: even if the call form is safe with respect to dynamic binding, a dependent import can still be invalidated because the covered symbol state changed.
Can you restate the hypothesis without turning it into an implementation decision or a proven result?

The hypothesis is that per-symbol fingerprints recording visibility, version, and prevailing definition provide a sound basis for invalidating imports dependent on a changed symbol, while calls that remain unchanged and dynamically bound match clean-build semantics. It proposes an invalidation boundary and a call-level safety claim; it does not yet establish either claim or declare all other cached work reusable.

To examine the visibility-and-binding question, I plan to enumerate ELF binding transitions and compare fingerprint-triggered invalidation against clean builds under LD_PRELOAD, dependency edits, and mixed optimization modes. How should I describe the purpose of that comparison?

It is a plan to test the proposed invalidation boundary, not a conclusion about it. Enumerating ELF binding transitions makes the changes in binding conditions explicit. For each relevant condition, the comparison asks whether an incremental build using fingerprint-triggered invalidation preserves the semantics of a clean build. LD_PRELOAD, dependency edits, and mixed optimization modes are the stated conditions under which to make that comparison.
When I say “enumerate ELF binding transitions,” am I claiming to know already which transitions invalidate imported IR?

No. The enumeration is part of finding out. It provides the changes to examine, including changes that may affect assumptions about symbol binding or preemptibility. The plan does not classify those transitions as safe or unsafe in advance.
Should the clean build be treated as another invalidation strategy?

No. A clean build is the semantic reference for the comparison; fingerprint-triggered invalidation is the proposed incremental behavior being examined. The question is whether the incremental result matches clean-build semantics under the stated conditions, not whether a clean build invalidates a cache in the same way.
What exactly would the fingerprint-triggered side of the comparison represent?

It represents reuse and invalidation governed by the proposed per-symbol fingerprints, which cover visibility, version, and prevailing definition. In this plan, you would compare the result of that approach with a clean build when the relevant conditions vary. That description does not assume the fingerprint rule succeeds or that those properties cover every possible dependency.
Does the plan require examining a change in visibility separately from a change in which definition prevails?

Enumerating binding transitions should make it possible to ask which property changed and which cached imports the fingerprint would treat as dependent. Visibility and prevailing definition are distinct properties named by the fingerprint hypothesis. The plan does not, however, state a completed list of transitions or prescribe that each property must be varied in isolation.
And version belongs in the fingerprint comparison even though the plan is phrased as ELF binding transitions?

Yes. The fingerprint hypothesis covers visibility, version, and prevailing definition, so comparing fingerprint-triggered invalidation calls for attending to the properties the fingerprint records. The plan's wording does not itself give a taxonomy of version changes or assert what any particular one would do.
Why is LD_PRELOAD singled out?

It supplies a stated condition for comparing behavior where dynamic symbol interposition may matter. The comparison should ask whether the incremental result under LD_PRELOAD has the same semantics as the corresponding clean build. Naming LD_PRELOAD does not, by itself, say that every symbol in every case is interposed or that any result already differs.
Would looking only at whether a call remains in the imported IR answer the LD_PRELOAD part?

Not completely. An unchanged dynamically bound call is part of the hypothesis being examined, but the comparison concerns the semantics of the resulting build. Imported IR could also embody assumptions beyond the presence of that call. The clean-build comparison is meant to expose whether fingerprint-triggered invalidation and reuse preserve the required behavior under LD_PRELOAD.
How do dependency edits fit if this is framed around symbol binding?

They are another explicit condition for the comparison. A dependency edit may affect information used by imported IR, including potentially relevant symbol properties, but the plan does not assert that every dependency edit does so. Comparing the incremental outcome with a clean build under dependency edits helps address whether the proposed invalidation remains sound when dependencies change.
Could I treat an unchanged fingerprint after a dependency edit as proof that cached imported IR is safe?

The plan does not establish that. A fingerprint reflects the symbol properties it covers; a dependency edit may be relevant for other reasons. The proposed comparison should not assume that an unchanged fingerprint alone settles semantic reuse. It asks whether the incremental behavior actually matches the clean-build reference under dependency edits.
What is the point of including mixed optimization modes in this same comparison?

It keeps the semantic check applicable when modules do not share one optimization mode. The plan asks whether fingerprint-triggered invalidation still yields clean-build semantics under mixed optimization modes, rather than assuming a result observed with uniform optimization would automatically carry over. It does not specify which modes are mixed or report an outcome.
Is this plan meant to measure the rebuild-time and runtime targets too?

The stated plan is specifically to enumerate ELF binding transitions and compare fingerprint-triggered invalidation with clean builds under LD_PRELOAD, dependency edits, and mixed optimization modes. It does not state a rebuild-time or runtime measurement procedure or claim those targets are met. Its immediate focus is the semantic soundness of the invalidation approach.
Suppose the incremental build and clean build behave the same for a case. Could I then say every ELF binding transition is handled?

No. Agreement in a particular comparison would speak to the condition examined, not to unexamined transitions. The point of enumeration is to make the set of transitions under consideration explicit, so the scope of any later conclusion is clear. At this stage, there are no comparison results to generalize.
And if a comparison were to differ, what would that say without jumping to a diagnosis?

Conditionally, a semantic difference would show that the incremental result did not match its clean-build reference in that case. It would not, by itself, identify whether the cause lay in the fingerprint's coverage, the determination of dependent imports, reuse of another assumption, or something else. The plan is to compare, not to preassign an explanation for a possible difference.
Does “fingerprint-triggered invalidation” imply invalidating all imported IR whenever any symbol changes?

No. The proposed rule concerns imports dependent on a symbol whose fingerprint changes. Comparing it with clean builds should keep that selective scope in view. The plan does not substitute global invalidation for the proposed rule, nor does it establish in advance that the chosen scope is sound.
Can we distinguish the two things I want to learn: when cached imports need invalidation and when a dynamically bound call can remain unchanged?

Yes. The transition enumeration helps pose the invalidation question for changes in ELF binding conditions. The clean-build comparisons ask whether fingerprint-triggered invalidation, together with any unchanged dynamically bound calls, preserves semantics under the specified conditions. A call's remaining dynamically bound and the validity of the entire cached import are related but distinct matters to examine.
Would it be accurate to say that LD_PRELOAD, dependency edits, and mixed optimization modes are three lenses on the same comparison rather than three answers?

Yes. They are conditions under which the plan proposes comparing the incremental result against clean builds. None is itself a finding that the fingerprint rule is sufficient or insufficient. The plan's answer to the visibility-and-binding question would depend on what those comparisons eventually show.
Please give me a compact formulation that still sounds like a plan.

Plan: enumerate ELF binding transitions, then compare incremental results using fingerprint-triggered invalidation with clean-build semantics under LD_PRELOAD, dependency edits, and mixed optimization modes. Use those comparisons to examine which binding changes require invalidation and when unchanged dynamically bound calls remain safe to reuse, without presuming the outcome.

Let's run the InterposeMatrix-120 binding-transition cases across dependency edits, mixed optimization modes, and LD_PRELOAD, and compare incremental outputs and traces against clean builds. What exactly is this activity checking?

It checks whether the incremental result behaves like the corresponding clean build in those binding-transition cases. Outputs and traces are the two stated bases for comparison. The activity evaluates the proposed reuse and invalidation behavior under dependency edits, mixed optimization modes, and LD_PRELOAD; it does not yet report what the comparisons show.
Should I describe InterposeMatrix-120 as the comparison itself, or as the set of cases we run?
Describe InterposeMatrix-120 as the named binding-transition cases being run. Comparing incremental outputs and traces with clean-build outputs and traces is what you do with those cases.
Why compare each incremental run with a clean build rather than compare incremental runs with one another?

The requirement is to preserve clean-build semantics. An incremental run can be consistent with another incremental run and still differ from the relevant clean build. Pairing each result with its clean-build counterpart makes that semantic reference explicit.
Does the clean-build counterpart need to reflect the same dependency edit and LD_PRELOAD condition?

Yes, for the comparison to address the stated question. The incremental and clean-build results should be compared under corresponding conditions. Otherwise, a difference could reflect different inputs or interposition conditions rather than a failure of incremental reuse. The activity statement does not prescribe the detailed setup for establishing that correspondence.
What do outputs and traces tell us separately?

Outputs let you compare the results produced by the two builds. Traces provide another view of their behavior that may reveal a difference not apparent from the outputs alone. The activity names both, but it does not specify a trace format or say that every difference between raw traces necessarily represents a semantic mismatch.
So I should not claim that identical outputs alone prove the cached imports were safe?

Correct. Identical outputs for a case would be one observation, while the stated activity also compares traces. Even agreement in both would be evidence about the cases and conditions examined, not an automatic proof about every possible binding transition or cached import.
Is the focus still on fingerprint-triggered invalidation?

Yes. The activity evaluates the proposal that per-symbol fingerprints covering visibility, version, and prevailing definition trigger invalidation of dependent imports, alongside the claim about unchanged dynamically bound calls. Running the cases and comparing against clean builds is how this activity examines those claims; it does not assume they hold.
When a dependency edit is involved, what is the comparison trying to catch?

I want to turn to the single-module-edit case. Which imported-function summaries need recomputation after one module changes, and which cached inlining decisions remain profitable?

That poses two related but distinct questions. First, which summaries used across module boundaries can no longer be relied on after the edit? Second, among cached inlining decisions that remain semantically permissible, which are still worth retaining for optimization benefit? The question does not yet identify a recomputation rule or a profitability test.
Why distinguish an imported-function summary from an inlining decision?

A summary is information about a function that another module may use. An inlining decision is a choice made using information available during optimization. A change could affect information underlying a decision, but the summary and the decision are not the same cached object. Asking about each separately helps avoid assuming that their reuse conditions are identical.
Does a change to one module mean every imported-function summary should be recomputed?

Not necessarily. The open question is which summaries are affected by that change. Recomputing everything would be a possible conservative response, but the wording asks for a boundary that distinguishes summaries requiring recomputation from those that do not. It does not establish where that boundary lies.
Could I say only summaries of functions defined in the edited module need work?

That would also be premature. A summary outside the edited module might rely on information that the edit changes, while a summary associated with the edited module might or might not be relevant to a particular importer. The question calls for determining the affected summaries rather than adopting a rule based solely on where each function is defined.
Are we asking whether the summary's source changed, or whether assumptions used to produce it changed?

Both are possible reasons to examine a summary. A direct change to what it describes may matter, and a change to information it relies on may matter even if its own module is unchanged. The question is about the conditions under which recomputation is necessary, without specifying a particular dependency-tracking mechanism.
What if a cached summary is no longer current but the inlining decision it informed happens to give the same behavior?

That possibility shows why the questions should not be collapsed. A decision's semantic validity, the currency of the summary used to reach it, and its continued profitability are different issues. The prompt does not give a rule for declaring that particular decision reusable merely because its behavior might happen to agree; it asks which decisions remain profitable after the change.
Is ‘profitable’ another way of saying ‘semantically safe’?

No. Semantic safety asks whether reuse preserves the required behavior. Profitability asks whether keeping an inlining decision still provides enough optimization benefit to be worthwhile. An inlining decision could be safe but no longer beneficial, or appear beneficial yet be impermissible to reuse. The question asks about cached decisions that remain profitable without waiving correctness.
Do we have a profitability threshold for an individual inlining decision?

Not in this question. It asks which cached decisions remain profitable but supplies no per-decision numerical threshold or ranking criterion. The broader runtime comparison with full LTO is a goal for the resulting build, not automatically a profitability rule for each individual inlining decision.
Would an unchanged imported-function summary prove that a previous inlining decision is still profitable?

No. An unchanged summary might preserve information relevant to making the decision, but profitability can depend on more than the mere fact that a summary did not change. The question leaves open how to assess whether a cached inlining choice remains advantageous under the changed build conditions.
Could a summary need recomputation without requiring every inlining decision that once used it to be discarded?

Conceptually, yes. Recomputing information and reassessing decisions are separate operations. The recomputed summary could conceivably leave some decisions justified and worthwhile, while affecting others. That is a possible distinction to examine, not a reported outcome or a prescribed reuse policy.
Could an unchanged summary coexist with an inlining decision that should be reconsidered?

It could in principle, if some condition relevant to that decision is not captured by the summary's unchanged state. That is why the question should ask what each cached decision depended on rather than treating a summary match as a universal certificate of profitability.
Should we treat inlining as automatically better whenever it was chosen before the edit?

No. ‘Remain profitable’ explicitly asks whether the earlier choice is still worthwhile after the module changes. A prior choice is not, by itself, evidence of present profitability. Nor does that wording claim that a prior choice has become unprofitable; it leaves the determination open.
Does the phrase ‘after one module changes’ restrict the question to changes inside an imported function?

No. It identifies a single-module change as the scenario, without limiting which part of that module changed. The relevant issue is whether the change affects a summary or an inlining decision's assumptions. The question supplies no particular edit or affected function.
What should I avoid assuming about the number of dependents affected by one module change?

Avoid assuming the affected set has a fixed size. ‘One module changes’ counts the edited modules, not the number of summaries or inlining decisions that might depend on the edit. The question is precisely about identifying which ones require work or remain reusable and profitable.
Is the objective to maximize reuse, even if that means keeping an unprofitable inline?

No. Reuse is useful only insofar as it supports the optimizer's correctness and performance aims. The question explicitly asks which cached inlining decisions remain profitable, so it does not equate retaining more decisions with producing a better result.

Does ‘changed summaries’ mean every summary in the module I edited?

Not necessarily. The hypothesis says to recompute changed summaries, not to classify every summary in the edited module as changed. It leaves open how the affected summaries are identified and whether a particular edit changes any given summary.
Could a summary in another module be among the transitive consumers?

The term ‘transitive consumers’ allows for consumers reached through more than one dependency step; it does not confine them to the edited module or to immediate importers. Whether a particular summary or optimization belongs to that set depends on its actual dependence on the changed information.

Am I claiming that every transitive consumer will produce a different result after recomputation?

No. Recomputing a consumer because its inputs may have changed is different from predicting that its output will change. The hypothesis identifies a scope of work to reconsider; it does not give counts or outcomes for individual consumers.

No particular representation is specified. The hypothesis links binding-aware fingerprints with recomputation of changed summaries and transitive consumers, but it does not prescribe how dependencies are recorded, traversed, or checked.
What qualifies an inlining decision as ‘unaffected’?

At the level of this hypothesis, it is a cached inlining decision whose relevant assumptions have not been changed by the edit or by binding conditions it depends on. Could an inlining decision in an unchanged module still be affected?

Yes, conceptually. If the decision depended on a changed imported summary or on a changed binding assumption, the module holding it could remain unchanged while the decision requires reconsideration. The proposed distinction is dependency-based, not simply a distinction between edited and unedited modules.
And could an inlining decision associated with the edited module still be retained?

The hypothesis does not rule that out solely because of its location. The condition it proposes is that the decision be unaffected. Whether a particular decision associated with the edited module meets that condition cannot be determined from the fact of a single-module edit alone.
Is ‘retain unaffected inlining’ a claim that every retained inline is individually profitable?

Does ‘within 5%’ refer to how many inlining decisions we retain?
No. The 5% comparison is about program runtime relative to full LTO. It is not a percentage of retained decisions, recomputed summaries, or modules that are optimized.

Does the hypothesis say that this approach halves full-LTO rebuild time for a single-module edit?

If a binding fingerprint changes but an inlining decision looks unaffected by the edited function, should it automatically be kept?

Not automatically. ‘Unaffected’ must include the decision's relevant binding assumptions. No. The summary could change for reasons other than a binding change. Binding-aware fingerprints are part of the proposed reuse boundary, but an unchanged binding fingerprint is not, on its own, a guarantee that every summary and every dependent inlining decision remains valid.

Yes. They refer to different affected sets. The hypothesis calls for recomputing changed summaries and their transitive consumers while retaining inlining decisions that remain unaffected. It does not propose retaining a decision whose supporting information requires reconsideration merely to save work.
Would recomputing transitive consumers mean recomputing all cross-module optimization?

Not by the wording of the hypothesis. ‘Transitive’ follows relevant dependencies; it does not mean ‘all.’ The affected set could be broad in a particular situation, but the hypothesis makes no claim about its size after any specific single-module edit.
How strongly should I state that retaining the unaffected inlines preserves performance?

State it as the performance part of the hypothesis: retaining unaffected inlining decisions is expected to keep runtime within 5% of full LTO. Avoid saying that this runtime bound has already been observed or that the retained decisions alone guarantee it in every build.

The hypothesis is that binding-aware fingerprints allow changed imported-function summaries and their transitive consumers to be recomputed after a single-module edit, while unaffected cached inlining decisions can be retained without pushing runtime more than 5% above full LTO.

I’d like a complementary proposal: prioritize profile-hot cross-module imports in bounded ThinLTO partitions, retain indirect calls for preemptible symbols, and treat unoptimized modules conservatively. How do those three choices work together?

They divide the proposal into optimization focus, work scope, and semantic constraints. Profile-hot imports are the cross-module opportunities to prioritize; bounded ThinLTO partitions limit the scope of that work. Retaining indirect calls for preemptible symbols avoids turning a potentially interposed call into an assumed fixed binding. Treating unoptimized modules conservatively avoids relying on optimization assumptions that may not apply to them. This is a proposed design, not a measured outcome.
What does “profile-hot” commit us to saying about an import?

It means the profile identifies the import as hot enough to prioritize. It does not state a numerical hotness threshold, name a particular profile, or establish how much runtime benefit that import will produce. Priority is a choice about where to focus cross-module optimization effort, not a guarantee that every selected import pays off.
And what makes an import cross-module in this wording?

The relevant optimization uses information or IR from another module. The proposal focuses on which such imports receive priority; it does not require importing every available function or specify exactly what material each import contains.
Why prioritize rather than simply say to import all profile-hot functions?

“Prioritize” leaves room for the bound on ThinLTO partitions and for correctness constraints. It says hot opportunities should receive attention ahead of less promising ones, without promising that every hot import will occur or that a profile indication overrides a binding restriction.
What does the bound on ThinLTO partitions actually specify?

It specifies that the partitions used for this cross-module work should have a limit. The proposal gives no numerical partition size, import budget, partitioning algorithm, or rule for assigning modules to partitions. The important stated property is bounded scope, not a particular bound.
Is the point of bounding partitions to make a single-module edit affect exactly one partition?

That is not promised. Bounding a partition limits its scope, but it does not establish that an edit affects only one partition or that there are no dependencies between partitions. The proposal can be motivated by limiting incremental work without asserting an exact invalidation boundary.
Could a hot import cross a partition boundary?

The proposal does not define the mechanics of partition boundaries or which imports can cross them. It says to prioritize profile-hot cross-module imports in bounded ThinLTO partitions. Whether a particular import fits within the applicable bounds would have to be determined by a design that implements the proposal.

Prioritizing profile-hot imports aims to preserve valuable cross-module optimization while work is bounded, which is relevant to that runtime target. But no runtime result is provided here. Whether the resulting program stays within 5% of full-LTO runtime remains to be assessed.
Is hotness allowed to override the rule about preemptible symbols? A very hot call might look attractive to make direct.

No. The proposal explicitly retains indirect calls for preemptible symbols. A profile can affect priority among permissible opportunities, but it cannot by itself justify assuming fixed binding for a call whose preemptibility must be preserved.

That reflects the call-level rule stated here: retain indirect calls for preemptible symbols. Avoid extending it into claims about exact instructions or about all optimization surrounding those calls. The proposal specifies the binding constraint, not a complete code-generation policy.
Does retaining the indirect call rule out importing information about the called function?

The proposal does not state such a blanket prohibition. It says to prioritize certain cross-module imports while keeping calls to preemptible symbols indirect. It does not specify which other uses of that information are permissible.

How should I interpret ‘treat unoptimized modules conservatively’ without inventing a precise policy?

Treat it as a constraint on assumptions: the optimizer should not rely on an unoptimized module having undergone transformations or providing guarantees that its optimization mode does not warrant. Then conservative treatment is not the same as treating an unoptimized module as absent?

Correct. The stated goal includes mixtures of optimized and unoptimized modules. Conservative treatment means respecting that mixture when making cross-module assumptions, not pretending an unoptimized module is missing from the program.
Does the proposal imply that unoptimized modules never benefit from cross-module information?

No. It does not give a blanket rule about benefits or forbid every interaction with them. It only says to treat them conservatively. A more specific rule about which imports or optimizations involving an unoptimized module are allowed is not supplied.

They can constrain the same opportunity without contradicting each other. No. The proposal does not decide that specific case. It requires retaining indirect calls for preemptible symbols and treating unoptimized modules conservatively, even when an import is profile-hot. Whether some cross-module work remains possible under those constraints is left open.

No. A partition bound limits the scope of work; it does not prove that cached information remains valid when a dependency changes. Clean-build semantics under dependency changes still requires sound reuse decisions. This proposal adds priorities and constraints, not a complete cache-validity test.

Yes. That is a general reading of ‘bounded.’ It should not be strengthened into a specific work limit, a guaranteed rebuild-time reduction, or a claim that all changes stay within one partition. None of those details is stated.

Exactly. A profile can guide optimization effort toward hot imports, while calls to preemptible symbols still remain indirect and unoptimized modules are still handled conservatively. The prioritization does not relax the requirement to match clean-build semantics.

Prioritize profile-hot cross-module imports within bounded ThinLTO partitions, while retaining indirect calls for preemptible symbols and treating unoptimized modules conservatively. No such benchmark inventory is specified. The plan says to benchmark single-module edits. It does not give a module count, prescribe particular edits, or claim that any benchmark has already been run.

Because the target is conditional: after a single-module edit, rebuild time should be at most 50% of a full-LTO rebuild time. The plan does not state that same numerical limit for every kind of change or for a clean build from scratch.
Is ‘at most 50% of full-LTO rebuild time’ exactly the earlier halving target?

Yes. If the full-LTO rebuild takes a given amount of time under a comparable setup, the planned incremental rebuild target is no more than half that time for a single-module edit. The percentage is a target, not a measured result.

The stated performance baseline is full-LTO runtime. Clean builds serve as the semantic reference for correctness; they do not replace full LTO as the runtime baseline in this target. What does ‘at most 5% runtime regression’ mean numerically?

Relative to full-LTO runtime, it means the resulting program should take no more than 1.05 times as long to run under a comparable measurement. It does not refer to a 5% change in rebuild time or to retaining 95% of the imports.
If the rebuild is 45% of full LTO but runtime is 7% slower, would that meet the tuning targets?

In that hypothetical comparison, it would meet the rebuild-time limit but miss the runtime-regression limit. The plan calls for satisfying both: rebuild time no more than 50% of the full-LTO baseline and runtime regression no more than 5%. Those hypothetical numbers are an illustration, not reported data.
What if runtime matches full LTO but the incremental rebuild takes 60% as long?

That hypothetical result would satisfy the runtime limit but miss the rebuild-time limit. A strong runtime result does not compensate for exceeding the specified rebuild-time bound; the two limits remain separate.
Does tuning mean we can sacrifice clean-build semantics to get under 50%?

No. The optimizer still has to match clean-build semantics under dependency changes, dynamic symbol interposition, and mixed optimized/unoptimized modules. The performance limits are to be pursued within that correctness requirement, not by relaxing it.
Where do preemptible calls fit in a plan focused on profiles and benchmarks?

Profile ranking and partition tuning cannot authorize assuming a fixed target where a call must remain preemptible. The plan addresses performance choices, while sound symbol-binding behavior remains a constraint on those choices. This node does not propose a new rule for representing or transforming calls.
Can an unoptimized module be excluded from the benchmarks to make the tuning easier?

The plan does not prescribe a benchmark mix or an exclusion policy. Whatever is benchmarked, the design’s correctness requirement still covers mixtures of optimized and unoptimized modules. A performance measurement in one arrangement should not be described as establishing results for an unmeasured arrangement.
Am I committing to one fixed ranking and cap before measuring anything?

No. Ranking imports and capping partitions are the choices to apply and tune. The plan does not state a final ordering, cap value, or selection rule. Benchmarking single-module edits provides the proposed basis for evaluating the rebuild-time side of those choices.
Could I claim that prioritizing profile-hot imports will keep runtime within 5%?

Not yet. Prioritizing them is a proposed way to preserve valuable optimization while limiting work. Whether that strategy keeps the resulting runtime within 5% of full LTO is precisely something the plan calls for assessing and tuning.
Does the benchmark need to time the resulting program as well as the rebuild?

To assess both stated tuning limits, you need a rebuild-time comparison and a runtime comparison for the resulting program. The plan names benchmarking single-module edits and tuning for both limits, but does not specify a detailed timing procedure, workload, or measurement protocol.
What should I avoid inferring from a rebuild-time number alone?

It cannot establish that runtime regression is at most 5%, or that the incremental result preserves clean-build semantics. Rebuild time is only one of the plan’s measurements. A faster rebuild is not a substitute for either optimization quality or correctness.
And what should I avoid inferring from a runtime number alone?

It cannot establish that a single-module edit rebuilds in at most 50% of full-LTO rebuild time, or that cache reuse remains sound under the stated binding and dependency conditions. Runtime is the separate performance comparison for the program produced.

Not from that one hypothetical observation. It would describe the measured edit and configuration, while the target is phrased for single-module edits generally. The plan gives no completed measurements or stated rule for generalizing from one benchmark case.

No. Full LTO is the comparison baseline for rebuild time and runtime. The planned optimization work uses profile-ranked imports and capped ThinLTO partitions; the plan does not say that the incremental build itself performs a full-LTO rebuild.

A symbol reference alone does not identify which provider the cached partition assumed would prevail. Including the prevailing provider makes that assumption part of the proposed reuse condition. If the provider changes, a partition that depended on the former provider should not be treated as having the same key merely because the symbol name is unchanged.
What does optimization mode contribute if the prevailing provider is already recorded?

The two fields answer different questions. The prevailing-provider field identifies the provider; the optimization-mode field records the optimization condition associated with the relevant work. The hypothesis is that distinguishing those conditions matters when deciding whether cached partition work can be carried across a provider replacement.
Does that imply every optimized-to-unoptimized replacement changes the prevailing provider field?

Not necessarily. The proposal names both the prevailing provider and optimization mode so the key can distinguish relevant changes in either property. It does not assume one field always changes whenever the other does.

The hypothesis treats symbol version as another resolution property a cached partition may have relied on. Recording it avoids treating two conditions with different relevant versions as interchangeable solely because the provider and mode appear unchanged. The hypothesis does not specify how versions are represented or which individual version changes affect a particular partition.

It captures the preemptibility condition relevant to a cached binding assumption as affected by -Bsymbolic state. The important distinction is between recording a provider and recording whether a call or use may safely assume that provider is fixed. The hypothesis proposes putting that distinction into the partition key; it does not define an encoding for it.

Not exactly as worded. The hypothesis specifies -Bsymbolic-derived preemptibility: the binding property relevant to reuse, as derived from that setting. It does not prescribe storing a raw flag, nor does it say that the same preemptibility value applies to every use in a partition.
Could a partition have the same prevailing provider and symbol version but a different preemptibility condition?

That is the kind of distinction the proposed fields are intended to preserve. Identifying a provider and version does not, on its own, establish that cached uses may bind to that provider unconditionally. If the relevant preemptibility condition changes, the key should be able to distinguish the two situations under the hypothesis.
Should I describe the four fields as four independent reasons to throw away every cached partition?

No. They are proposed components of keys for partitions whose cached work depends on them. The hypothesis is about preventing reuse under an incompatible key, not globally discarding every partition whenever any provider, mode, version, or preemptibility condition changes. It does not specify the precise granularity of the affected set.
What if one field changes but the cached partition never relied on that particular symbol?

The proposed key should be understood in relation to the partition’s relevant dependencies. A change unrelated to its cached work does not, merely by existing, establish that its binding assumptions are stale. The hypothesis does not yet spell out how relevant dependencies are identified or represented within a partition key.
Does a matching partition key prove the cached optimization is safe to reuse?

Not on its own. A match would indicate agreement on the properties captured by the key as applied to that partition. Reuse can also depend on other information, and the hypothesis has not shown that these four fields exhaust every relevant condition. The specific claim here is that they would eliminate the MixedMode-90 misbindings.
If the key changes, are we claiming the program’s behavior must change?

No. A changed key is a reason, under the hypothesis, not to reuse cached work on the old assumptions. It does not predict that the rebuilt program will necessarily have different observable behavior. Cache invalidation and a behavioral difference are separate claims.
Does this hypothesis require replacing a partition with a wholly new one whenever its key changes?

It proposes distinguishing conditions for reuse, but does not specify the subsequent rebuilding or reoptimization procedure. You can say an old cached partition should not be reused under an incompatible key without prescribing how much work must then be redone.
Could I say the key prevents a profile-hot ranking from masking a binding change?

Yes, as an explanation of the proposed separation of concerns. Profile hotness makes an import attractive to optimize; it does not make old binding assumptions valid. The proposed key would condition reuse on the named provider, mode, version, and preemptibility information even for a partition whose imports remain profile-hot.

No. It concerns the validity of cached profile-hot partitions under linker-resolution and optimization-mode changes. It does not provide a profile ranking, a partition cap, or a measure of an import’s benefit.
When an unoptimized provider replaces an optimized one, which part of the key is supposed to notice?

The prevailing-provider and optimization-mode components are the immediately relevant named distinctions. No. The hypothesis proposes a key covering all four properties, not a result for optimization mode alone. A mode label does not by itself specify which provider prevails, the relevant symbol version, or whether an assumed fixed binding remains permissible.

Yes, unless the counting convention establishes that each mismatch corresponds to a distinct swap. The exact reported figures—3, 2, 1, and 0 trace mismatches across 400 swaps—are clear without that extra assumption.
Can I say the combined configuration improves symbol-resolution correctness over the other three?

You can say it had fewer mismatches against clean-build traces than each of the other three configurations in the examined swaps. That is a precise comparison of the reported binding-behavior measure. Calling it universally correct would extend the result beyond those traces and conditions.
Does this result measure how fast the four configurations rebuild?

No. It supplies trace-mismatch counts, not rebuild seconds or ratios against full-LTO rebuild time. The zero-mismatch configuration may differ in rebuild work, but no rebuild-time result is stated here.
What about program runtime or retained inlining?

Neither is measured in this finding. There is no full-LTO program-runtime ratio and no result about the profitability of retained inlining. The evidence concerns clean-build trace agreement across the provider-swap ablation.
Can a trace mismatch be offset by better rebuild performance?

No. The trace comparison addresses whether incremental symbol-resolution behavior agrees with clean builds; rebuild speed is a separate measure. This result reports no rebuild speed to weigh in any event.
If someone asks whether the result proves that snapshot refresh catches versioned imports and alias keys catch unversioned ones, what is the precise response?

The four aggregate counts do not establish that assignment. They show that neither safeguard alone yielded zero mismatches and that the combined configuration did in these 400 swaps. Although the activity called for a versioned-versus-unversioned breakdown, that breakdown is not present in this evidence statement.

The reported totals do not tell us. The same underlying swap or import might contribute a mismatch under more than one configuration, or the sets might differ. Without case-level information, avoid treating the four mismatch counts as disjoint or as a list of individually tracked failures.
Is there a concise conclusion that does not imply the two safeguards were independently proven necessary?

Yes: across the 400 provider swaps, only the configuration with both linker-snapshot refresh and default-alias keys had zero clean-build trace mismatches; the configurations with neither, alias keys only, and refresh only had 3, 2, and 1, respectively. That is the observed four-way comparison, without a broader necessity claim.

The description says it tabulates refreshed snapshot hashes, but does not specify their placement across all four configurations. Avoid asserting a per-configuration hash layout that is not stated.
